rw: When supply rises and demand stays the same, the supply curve shifts right, creating a surplus at the old price, so competition among sellers pushes the equilibrium price lower.

ww.The price stays the same because demand: The price does not stay fixed here, because a rise in supply alone shifts the supply curve right and moves the market to a new, lower price.
ww.The price rises to a record because sell: Sellers gaining more goods to sell does not give them pricing power; extra supply against unchanged demand pushes sellers to compete, so the price falls rather than rising.
ww.The price tends to rise because there is: A larger amount for sale pushes the price down, not up, because buyers are no more eager than before and sellers must cut prices to clear the extra goods.

rw: A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded at a given price, leaving unsold goods on the shelves, which usually pushes the price down toward equilibrium.

ww.Quantity demanded exceeds quantity suppl: This describes a shortage, not a surplus; a surplus is the reverse, where quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, leaving sellers rather than buyers without a match.
ww.A situation in which the price of a good: A price equal to the cost of production says nothing about quantities, so it is not a surplus; a surplus is defined by supply exceeding demand at a price.
ww.A situation in which the government buys: Government purchases of all goods offered is a policy such as price support, not the definition of a surplus; a surplus is simply supply exceeding demand at a price.

rw: A shortage occurs when quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at a given price, so some buyers cannot get the good, which tends to push the price upward.

ww.A situation in which a firm has more cas: Having extra cash is a business finance situation and has nothing to do with quantities in a market; a shortage means buyers want more than sellers offer.
ww.A situation in which the government sets: A government limit on price is a price ceiling, which can cause a shortage but is not the definition of one; a shortage is demand exceeding supply at a price.
ww.Quantity supplied exceeds quantity deman: This describes a surplus, where sellers have leftover goods; a shortage is the opposite, with buyers wanting more than the quantity supplied at that price.

rw: A complementary good is used together with another good, such as printers and ink, so when demand for one rises, demand for the other usually rises too.

ww.A good that has no value to customers an: A good with no value that is never sold is not a complement; complements have real value because they are consumed together with another product that buyers want.
ww.A good that is given away free to custom: A free gift with a purchase is a promotion, not a complement; complements are separate goods normally bought and used together, such as bread and butter.
ww.A good that can be used in place of anot: That describes a substitute, which can be used in place of another good when its price rises; complements are used together rather than swapped for each other.

rw: A normal good is one whose demand rises as consumer incomes rise, because people with more income buy more of it, such as restaurant meals or new clothing.

ww.A good that has no price because the gov: A good with no price supplied free by government is a public provision; normal goods are ordinary market goods defined by how demand responds to rising income.
ww.A good that is bought by every consumer: Identical yearly purchases by every consumer is not how normal goods work; their demand varies, rising when consumer incomes rise, so amounts bought are not fixed.
ww.A good whose demand falls as consumers': A good whose demand falls as income rises is an inferior good, the opposite of a normal good, because buyers switch to better alternatives when they can afford them.

rw: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large sellers, such as airlines or car makers, where each firm reacts to the pricing choices of its rivals.

ww.A market with thousands of small sellers: Thousands of small sellers offering identical products describes perfect competition, not an oligopoly, which has only a few large firms controlling most of the market.
ww.A market with one seller and no close su: One seller with no close substitutes is a monopoly; an oligopoly has a few sellers, so several firms share the market and watch one another.
ww.A market in which the government sets th: Government setting every price describes a command economy, not a market structure; an oligopoly is about the number of sellers, which is a few large firms.

rw: The unemployment rate is the number of jobless people looking for work divided by the labor force, which includes both employed and unemployed people who are able and seeking jobs.

ww.The share of workers who work part time: That describes underemployment, where part-time workers want more hours; the unemployment rate counts only people with no job who are actively searching, divided by the labor force.
ww.The share of workers who earn the minimu: Minimum wage earners all have jobs, so they are employed and not counted as unemployed; the rate concerns jobless people actively searching for work, not low wages.
ww.The share of all people in the country w: The rate divides by the labor force, not by the whole population, so children and retirees who are not seeking work are excluded from both parts of the calculation.

rw: The circular flow model shows how money, goods and resources move between households and firms, with households supplying labor and buying products while firms pay wages and sell output.

ww.A model showing how prices rise in a spi: A wage and price spiral is inflation, which is a different idea; the circular flow model shows exchanges between households and firms, not prices rising over time.
ww.A model showing how a bank moves money b: Moving money between branches of one bank is a banking operation, not an economic model; the circular flow follows exchanges among households, firms and markets in the whole economy.
ww.A model showing the path that a delivery: A delivery truck route is a logistics matter, not economics; the circular flow model tracks money, goods and resources moving between households and firms, not a physical driving path.

rw: A subsidy is a payment from the government to support a producer or activity, which lowers production costs and can raise output, such as farm support payments.

ww.A fine the government charges to a busin: A fine charged to rule breakers is a penalty paid to the government; a subsidy flows the other way, as a payment from the government to producers.
ww.A tax the government charges on goods th: A charge on imports is a tariff, which collects money from importers; a subsidy is money paid out by government to support producers or an activity, not collected.
ww.A fee the government charges for a licen: A license fee is money paid to the government for permission to operate; a subsidy reverses this flow because the government pays money to the producer instead.

rw: In a command economy the government makes most decisions about production and prices, using central planning instead of market forces to decide what, how and for whom to produce.

ww.Individuals and firms make most decision: Decisions guided by markets, prices and profit describe a market economy; in a command economy the government, not private firms and consumers, decides what is produced.
ww.Customs and habits passed down through g: Customs and habits passed down through generations describe a traditional economy; a command economy is run by government planners who set production targets and prices.
ww.Private firms make all decisions while t: A system where private firms decide everything and government has no role is pure laissez-faire; a command economy is the opposite, with the state controlling most decisions.

rw: A traditional economy is guided by customs and habits passed down through generations, with roles such as farming or hunting inherited, so decisions follow established practice rather than markets or plans.

ww.The government makes most decisions abou: Government decisions about production and prices describe a command economy; a traditional economy relies on custom and inherited roles instead of any central planning authority.
ww.Firms and the government share decisions: Sharing decisions between firms and the government describes a mixed economy; a traditional economy depends on long-standing customs rather than markets or public rules.
ww.Prices and profit guide the decisions of: Prices and profit guiding free markets describes a market economy; in a traditional economy, customs and habits, not price signals, determine who produces what.

rw: A mixed economy combines private choice with government involvement, as in most modern countries where firms and consumers use markets while the state regulates, taxes and provides some services.

ww.All decisions are made by private firms: Private firms deciding everything with no state role describes a pure market economy; a mixed economy combines private choice with a meaningful amount of government involvement.
ww.Customs and habits decide all outcomes a: Customs deciding all outcomes with no markets describes a traditional economy; a mixed economy blends market choices with government rules, so it does include markets.
ww.The government owns all firms and decide: A government owning all firms and setting every price is a command economy; a mixed economy leaves much production to private firms alongside some state action.

rw: Private property is the right of individuals and firms to own and use resources, which gives them incentives to work, invest and take care of what they own.

ww.The right of the government to seize any: Private property rights protect owners from arbitrary seizure; a government seizing assets at will without payment would destroy those rights, so it is the opposite of private property.
ww.The rule that only wealthy families may: Private property is open to all individuals and firms, not restricted to wealthy families; limiting ownership to the rich is not part of how market economies define it.
ww.The rule that all land and factories bel: Community ownership of all land and factories describes collective or socialist ownership; private property in a market economy means individuals and firms hold ownership, not the whole community.

rw: A key advantage of a market economy is that prices and competition encourage efficiency and innovation, since firms that cut costs or improve products earn profit and win customers.

ww.The government sets the price of every g: A government setting every price describes a command economy and is not an advantage of markets; in a market economy, prices come from supply and demand.
ww.Everyone is guaranteed the same income w: Guaranteeing equal income regardless of effort removes incentives to work and is not how markets operate; markets reward work and skill with different incomes.
ww.A central plan removes all waste because: A central plan describes a command economy, and one office cannot know what every person needs, so it does not eliminate waste and is not a market advantage.

rw: A key disadvantage of a market economy is income inequality and little provision of public goods, since profit-seeking firms undersupply goods such as roads and defense that cannot be sold.

ww.The government sets the price of every g: Government price setting belongs to a command economy; in a market economy firms are free to compete, so this is not a disadvantage of markets.
ww.All firms are owned by the state and so: State ownership of all firms describes a command economy; in market economies firms are privately owned and profit motivates workers and owners, so this is not a market weakness.
ww.Customs decide who does each job, which: Customs deciding who does each job describes a traditional economy; market economies let people choose careers, so this is not a disadvantage of markets.

rw: A key disadvantage of a command economy is that planners may misjudge what people want, causing shortages of some goods and waste of others, because no price signals guide them.

ww.Prices change so quickly that firms cann: Rapidly changing prices that confuse firms are a feature of unstable market economies; in command economies the government sets prices, so they usually do not change quickly.
ww.Private firms earn too much profit and u: Private firms earning large profits belongs to market economies; in a command economy the state owns most firms, so private profit is not the main problem.
ww.Customs prevent any change in methods, s: Customs preventing change describes a traditional economy; a command economy is run by planners who direct production, so the slow progress is not caused by custom.

rw: Privatization is transferring a government-owned business to private owners, such as selling a state airline to investors, which shifts decisions and profits from the public sector to private hands.

ww.A person keeping a personal diary that n: Keeping a personal diary private is about personal privacy and has no connection to business ownership; privatization concerns who owns an enterprise, not who may read a diary.
ww.A firm making its financial records secr: A firm keeping financial records secret is about confidentiality, not ownership; privatization specifically means selling or handing state-run businesses over to private owners.
ww.The government taking over a private fir: The government taking over a private firm is nationalization, which is the opposite of privatization; privatization moves ownership from the public sector to private owners.

rw: Nationalization is the government taking ownership of a private industry, such as a state takeover of railways or utilities, putting those assets under public control.

ww.A firm selling its goods in every region: Selling at one national price is a pricing policy and does not change who owns the firm; nationalization concerns the government taking over ownership.
ww.A firm moving its factories to a foreign: Moving factories abroad for cheaper wages is offshoring, a location decision made by the firm; nationalization instead means the government takes ownership of a private industry.
ww.Transferring a government-owned business: A public sale of a government-owned business to private owners is privatization, which is the reverse of nationalization, where government takes over private companies.

rw: Governments regulate businesses to protect consumers, workers and the environment, through rules on product safety, wages and working conditions, and pollution that firms might ignore if left alone.

ww.To stop new firms from ever entering a m: Regulation does not aim to block all new firms; competition law actually tries to keep markets open, so stopping entry would harm consumers and is not the purpose.
ww.To raise the prices of all goods so that: Governments do not regulate in order to raise all prices; regulations such as safety and competition rules aim to protect people, and higher prices would hurt consumers.
ww.To make sure every business earns the sa: Guaranteeing equal profit for every business is not a goal of regulation; profits vary with efficiency and demand, while regulation targets safety, fairness and harm to others.

rw: A financial business handles money, such as a bank that takes deposits and lends, or an insurer that pools risk, rather than making or selling physical goods.

ww.A business that sells groceries to the p: Selling groceries in supermarkets is retail, a commerce business, not a financial one; financial businesses handle money, credit, savings or insurance rather than goods.
ww.A business that grows wheat and corn on: Growing wheat and corn is agriculture, a primary industry producing raw products; it is not a financial business, which deals in money services.
ww.A business that makes cars and trucks in: Making cars and trucks is manufacturing, a secondary industry that turns materials into goods; financial businesses instead provide services such as banking, lending and insurance.

rw: Outsourcing is hiring another company to perform tasks or services, such as payroll, customer support or manufacturing, so the firm can focus on its core work.

ww.Selling goods to customers abroad by ope: Opening a foreign branch to sell abroad is exporting or expansion, and the firm still does its own work; outsourcing means hiring another company to do tasks.
ww.Doing all work inside the firm with its: Doing all work inside the firm with its own staff and equipment is the opposite of outsourcing, which hands tasks to an outside company.
ww.Moving a factory to another city at home: Moving a factory to another city is relocation, still done by the firm itself; outsourcing means paying another company to perform a task or service.

rw: A supplier provides goods or materials to another business, such as a flour mill selling flour to a bakery, so the buyer has inputs to make its products.

ww.Competes with the firm for the same cust: A firm competing for the same customers is a competitor, not a supplier; suppliers help a business by providing inputs rather than fighting for its buyers.
ww.Lends the firm money for a fixed period: Lending money and charging interest is the role of a lender, such as a bank; a supplier provides goods or materials, not loans.
ww.Buys finished goods from stores and sell: Buying finished goods from stores and reselling them describes a middleman or reseller; a supplier sends goods or materials to businesses so they can operate.

rw: The main purpose of a business is to provide goods or services that meet needs and earn a profit, which rewards owners and lets the firm keep operating.

ww.To reduce the number of customers so tha: Reducing customers to lower the owner's workload defeats a business, which needs customers to earn revenue; its purpose is serving customers, not avoiding work.
ww.To give away goods and services to the p: Giving away goods at no cost would bring no revenue and cause losses, so it is a charity activity, not the main purpose of a business.
ww.To avoid paying taxes by spending all in: Spending all income to avoid taxes would leave no profit and is not a legitimate purpose; businesses aim to earn a profit and still pay taxes owed.

rw: Entrepreneurs can raise start-up funds from several sources, including personal savings, bank loans, investors and crowdfunding, which is why this broad answer is correct.

ww.Only from the government, since banks an: It is false that only the government funds start-ups, because banks and investors often lend to new businesses; the word only makes this option wrong.
ww.Only from a lottery prize that the owner: A lottery prize is a rare and unreliable source; it is not the only way to fund a start-up, since savings, loans and investors are common.
ww.Only from customers, who must pay for al: Customers prepaying for all goods before production is unrealistic and is not the only source; most firms use savings, loans, investors or crowdfunding.

rw: An entrepreneur starts and runs a business and takes on its risk, hoping to earn profit but also facing the chance of losing the money invested.

ww.A person who works for a fixed wage in a: A fixed-wage store worker with no say in running the business is an employee, not an entrepreneur, who starts the enterprise and bears the risk.
ww.A person who buys goods from a business: A person buying goods for personal use and not reselling them is a consumer, not an entrepreneur, who produces or sells goods to earn profit.
ww.A person who lends money to a business a: Someone who lends money and receives interest is an investor or lender; an entrepreneur starts and runs the business and takes the risk of its success or failure.

rw: A real risk entrepreneurs face is losing the money they invested if the business fails, since savings and loans can be lost when sales fall short of costs.

ww.A guaranteed profit every month, whateve: A guaranteed monthly profit is not a risk but a benefit, and no business has one, since weather, seasons and the economy affect earnings.
ww.Freedom from all legal responsibilities: Freedom from legal duties and taxes is not true, since businesses must obey laws and pay taxes; it describes no risk that entrepreneurs face.
ww.No competition ever, since new businesse: Having no competition for years is an advantage, not a risk, and rarely happens; competitors usually appear, and the risk comes from losses instead.

rw: A sole proprietor reports business income on the owner's personal tax return, because the business and the owner are legally the same person, so profit is taxed as personal income.

ww.The business pays corporate tax and the: Paying corporate tax and then tax again on dividends describes a C corporation with double taxation; a sole proprietorship does not have a separate taxable business entity.
ww.The business pays no tax of any kind on: Sole proprietors do pay tax; the profits are taxed as the owner's income, so neither the business nor the owner paying nothing is false.
ww.The business files a separate return and: A sole proprietorship does not file a separate return, and the owner is taxed on the profit through a personal return, so this option is wrong on both points.

rw: An apprenticeship combines paid on-the-job training with classroom learning, letting workers earn wages while building skills for a trade such as electrician or plumber.

ww.A loan for starting a business, paid bac: A loan for starting a business is a form of financing, not training; an apprenticeship is paid on-the-job training with classroom learning for a skilled trade.
ww.A permanent management role in a company: A permanent management role with a company car is a job, not training; apprenticeships are temporary learning programs that prepare workers for skilled occupations.
ww.A short course taken in a classroom with: An apprenticeship includes real work experience and pay, so a classroom-only course with no experience and no pay does not describe it.

rw: Networking in career planning means building contacts who can share job leads and advice, which helps people hear about openings and learn about careers they might want.

ww.Setting up computers in an office so tha: Setting up office computers is computer networking, which connects machines; networking in career planning means building human contacts who share job leads and advice.
ww.Applying for many jobs at once without s: Applying for many jobs without speaking to anyone is the opposite of networking, which depends on conversations and relationships with people in your field.
ww.Waiting for employers to call after send: Waiting for employers after one application is passive and involves no contacts; networking is the active process of building relationships that lead to job information.

rw: Benefits like health insurance and retirement matches add real value beyond salary, so a job with lower pay but stronger benefits can be worth more overall.

ww.Benefits reduce the number of hours that: Benefits do not reduce hours worked; they are compensation such as insurance or retirement contributions, so this does not explain why someone would accept lower pay.
ww.Benefits are paid only to workers who ea: Benefits are not restricted to the highest earners, since many employers offer them to all employees; this claim is false and gives no reason to accept lower pay.
ww.Benefits are always worthless to workers: Benefits such as insurance and retirement contributions have real long-term value, so calling them always worthless is false and cannot justify choosing lower pay.

rw: A performance review is a periodic evaluation of an employee's work, where a manager assesses results, gives feedback and sets goals, often influencing raises and promotions.

ww.A plan for a company party which the man: A company party plan is a social event and has nothing to do with judging work; a performance review is a periodic evaluation of an employee.
ww.A list of the reasons why an employee sh: A list of reasons for a raise is a request or argument by the employee; a performance review is an evaluation of the employee's work by the employer.
ww.A review of a product by a customer who: A customer's review of a product evaluates the product, not an employee; a performance review is conducted by an employer to assess an employee's work.

rw: A résumé is a summary of your education, skills and work experience, which employers use to decide whether to interview you for a job.

ww.A form that employers fill out to descri: A form describing a job's duties is a job description written by employers; a résumé is written by the applicant about their own background.
ww.A list of the company's products with th: A list of products and prices is a catalog or price list for customers; a résumé presents the applicant's education, skills and work experience to employers.
ww.A letter that thanks an interviewer for: A letter thanking an interviewer is a thank-you note sent after an interview; a résumé is a summary of the applicant's qualifications sent when applying.

rw: A cover letter introduces you and shows your fit for the job, explaining why your background suits the role and the employer, and encouraging them to read your résumé.

ww.To ask the employer for a higher salary: Asking for higher pay in a cover letter is inappropriate; salary is discussed later, and the letter should show why you fit the job instead.
ww.To list every job you ever had, with the: Listing every job with dates, pay and bosses is what a résumé or application does; a cover letter is a short introduction that highlights fit, not a full history.
ww.To complain about the way in which the c: Complaining about the company's treatment of its employees would damage your chances; a cover letter should be positive and show how you fit the job.

rw: A student with no work experience should include school activities, volunteering and relevant skills, since these show responsibility, teamwork and abilities employers value.

ww.Nothing at all, since employers do not h: Employers do hire people without work histories, such as students, who can show other strengths; including nothing at all would waste the chance to impress.
ww.Invented job titles and made-up skills t: Inventing job titles and skills is dishonest and may cost you the job if discovered; a résumé must be truthful, so fabrication is never acceptable.
ww.A list of games played, with scores and: A list of games and scores shows little about job skills; employers want relevant evidence of responsibility and ability, not a record of games played.

rw: Sending a thank-you message soon after an interview is a good next step, since it shows courtesy, repeats your interest and keeps your name in front of the employer.

ww.Post complaints about the company online: Posting complaints online after a day is unprofessional and could harm your reputation; employers need time to decide, so patience is the better course.
ww.Wait silently for a year in case the emp: Waiting silently for a year shows no interest and lets the employer forget you; sending a prompt thank-you message is the better follow-up.
ww.Call the interviewer every hour until yo: Calling the interviewer every hour is harassment and would annoy the employer, hurting your chances; a single polite thank-you message is appropriate.

rw: A behavioral interview question asks how you handled a past situation, such as a time you resolved a conflict, since past behavior helps predict future performance.

ww.A question asking what you would do in a: A question about what you would do in an imaginary case is a hypothetical or situational question, not a behavioral one, which asks about real past events.
ww.A question that asks only for your name: Asking only for name and birth date is a basic personal detail question, and birth date may be inappropriate; behavioral questions explore past actions at work.
ww.A question about your plans for the week: Questions about weekend plans and sports are small talk and not behavioral questions, which investigate how you acted in earlier work or school situations.

rw: Making eye contact and listening carefully shows respect, interest and good communication, which are professional behaviors that help an interviewer judge you favorably.

ww.Arriving ten minutes late and apologizin: Arriving ten minutes late and apologizing only if asked shows poor punctuality and carelessness; professional candidates arrive early and do not wait to be questioned about lateness.
ww.Checking your phone repeatedly while the: Checking your phone while the interviewer speaks is disrespectful and shows lack of interest, so it harms your impression instead of showing professionalism.
ww.Interrupting the interviewer so that you: Interrupting the interviewer is rude and suggests poor listening; professional candidates wait until the interviewer finishes before speaking and make their points at the right time.

rw: Asking whether you plan to have children is generally illegal because it relates to family status and sex, which anti-discrimination laws protect from hiring decisions.

ww.Whether you can work the hours that the: Asking whether you can work the hours the job requires is legal because it concerns the ability to do the essential duties, so it is allowed.
ww.Why you want this job and what skills yo: Asking why you want the job and what skills you bring is a normal and legal question, since it relates directly to your qualifications.
ww.What your career goals are for the next: Asking about career goals for the next five years is a common, legal question that focuses on your plans and ambition, not a protected characteristic.

rw: Employers conduct background checks to verify information and reduce hiring risks, such as confirming past jobs, education and records relevant to the position.

ww.To lower employee pay by finding faults: Background checks are not used to lower pay; they verify facts about applicants, and finding faults to cut salaries is not their purpose.
ww.To find reasons for refusing to hire any: Employers run checks to confirm facts and manage risk, not to look for excuses to reject everyone who applies; that purpose is unfair and untrue.
ww.To discover which applicants have the mo: Counting friends on social media is not a goal of background checks, which confirm facts like employment, education and criminal history that bear on job risk.

rw: The best response to praise is to say thank you and share credit with others who helped, showing gratitude, humility and good teamwork.

ww.Brag about it to everyone in the office: Bragging about praise to everyone is arrogant and annoys coworkers; a professional response is to be gracious and acknowledge others who helped.
ww.Ignore the praise and walk away without: Ignoring praise and walking away is rude and ungracious; the professional response is to thank the person for noticing your work.
ww.Say that the praise is not deserved and: Saying the praise is undeserved and the team did all the work denies your real contribution and is a false modesty; it is better to thank them.

rw: The freeze destroys oranges, so supply decreases and the supply curve shifts left; with demand unchanged, buyers compete for fewer oranges and the price of juice rises.

ww.The price falls because supply increases: A freeze that destroys oranges reduces supply rather than increasing it, because fewer oranges reach the market, so the price does not fall for that reason.
ww.The price falls because demand for juice: The freeze affects how much fruit is produced, not what consumers want, so demand for juice does not drop and does not cause a lower price.
ww.The price stays the same because the dem: Supply falls because the crop is destroyed, so the supply curve shifts left; with demand unchanged, the price changes, and it does not stay the same.

rw: A health study makes more people want the snack at every price, so the demand curve shifts to the right, which is an increase in demand.

ww.It stays in place because only price cha: Price changes cause movement along the curve, but tastes and information shift the whole curve; the health news changes tastes, so the curve does shift.
ww.It becomes vertical so that nobody can b: A demand curve does not become vertical because people begin buying more; vertical would mean quantity never responds to price, and buyers still can purchase the snack.
ww.It shifts to the left because fewer peop: A leftward shift means fewer people want the snack, but the study led more people to buy it, so demand increases and shifts right.

rw: A machine that doubles output with the same workers lowers the cost per pair, so the factory supplies more shoes at every price, and the supply curve shifts right.

ww.Supply disappears because shoes become t: Supply does not vanish when shoes become cheaper to make; lower costs encourage production, so the quantity supplied rises rather than falling to nothing.
ww.Supply stays the same because workers ar: The same workers can now produce twice as much, so technology matters more than the number of workers; supply does change by increasing, not staying the same.
ww.Supply decreases because the factory nee: The machine increases productivity, so the factory makes more shoes, not fewer; needing fewer workers lowers cost, which raises supply rather than decreasing it.

rw: A normal good is one whose demand rises as consumer incomes rise, and restaurant meals fit because higher incomes lead people to eat out more often.

ww.Capital good: A capital good is a tool or machine used to produce other goods, and restaurant meals are consumed by households, so they are not capital goods.
ww.Inferior good: An inferior good loses demand when incomes rise, but demand for restaurant meals increased as incomes rose, so they are not inferior goods.
ww.Public good: A public good, such as national defense, is nonrival and nonexcludable; restaurant meals are sold to paying customers, so they are private goods, not public goods.

rw: Instant noodles are an inferior good because demand falls as incomes rise, with people switching to fresh food they prefer once they can afford it.

ww.Luxury good: A luxury good is a normal good whose demand rises strongly with income; instant noodles fall in demand when income rises, so they are not luxuries.
ww.Normal good, since demand for it rises w: A normal good has demand that rises with income, but people buy fewer noodles as their income rises, so this option contradicts the facts given.
ww.Public good: A public good is available to everyone without being sold to individuals, like street lighting; instant noodles are sold in stores, so they are not public goods.

rw: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a change in price, so a large response means demand is elastic and a small one means inelastic.

ww.How quickly prices rise each year across: Rising prices across the economy measured by an index describes inflation, not elasticity, which measures how much buyers change quantity in response to one good's price change.
ww.How much a good costs to make in a facto: Production cost in a factory concerns the supply side, while elasticity of demand describes how buyers react to a change in price, not what making a good costs.
ww.How much a firm earns when it sells at a: Earnings at a fixed price describe revenue, but elasticity is about how quantity demanded changes when price changes, so a fixed price excludes the key idea.

rw: Insulin for a diabetic has inelastic demand because it is a necessity with no substitutes, so people keep buying nearly the same quantity even if the price rises sharply.

ww.A specific brand of potato chips sold in: A brand of chips with many close substitutes has elastic demand, since buyers switch to other brands when its price rises, so it is not inelastic.
ww.A luxury cruise: A luxury cruise is a discretionary purchase that people can delay or skip when prices rise, so demand is elastic and not inelastic.
ww.A particular movie ticket: A particular movie ticket has many substitutes such as streaming or other entertainment, and it is not a necessity, so demand is fairly elastic, not inelastic.

rw: A specific soda brand with many alternatives has elastic demand, because when its price rises buyers readily switch to other drinks, and quantity demanded falls sharply.

ww.Gasoline for a daily commuter with no al: A commuter with no alternative must keep buying gasoline even when prices rise, so quantity demanded barely changes and demand is inelastic, not elastic.
ww.Prescription medicine for a chronic illn: Medicine for a chronic illness is a necessity with no easy substitute, so patients keep buying despite price increases and demand is inelastic, not elastic.
ww.Table salt: Table salt is cheap, a necessity and has few substitutes, so buyers hardly change quantity when its price rises, making demand inelastic rather than elastic.

rw: With elastic demand, a price rise cuts quantity demanded by a larger percentage than the price increase, so total revenue (price times quantity) falls.

ww.It stays the same in all cases: Revenue does not stay the same in all cases; it depends on elasticity, and with elastic demand the lost sales outweigh the higher price, so revenue falls.
ww.It becomes zero: Revenue becomes zero only if nobody buys at all; with elastic demand, quantity falls by a large amount but not to zero, so revenue falls but stays positive.
ww.It rises because price is higher: A higher price raises revenue only when demand is inelastic; with elastic demand the drop in quantity is proportionally larger, so total revenue falls despite the higher price.

rw: With inelastic demand, quantity sold falls proportionally less than price rises, so price times quantity increases and total revenue rises after the price increase.

ww.It becomes zero: Revenue does not become zero, because buyers with inelastic demand keep purchasing most of the quantity even at a higher price, so sales continue.
ww.It stays the same: Revenue changes in this case, because inelastic demand means quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so the result is not the same as before.
ww.It falls because fewer units are sold: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so the lost sales do not outweigh the higher price and revenue does not fall.

rw: A maximum rent below equilibrium makes the quantity of housing demanded exceed the quantity supplied, producing a shortage of rental housing with more renters than available units.

ww.A rise in the quality of every unit: A price ceiling below the market price does not improve quality; sellers earn less and often reduce maintenance, so quality tends to fall rather than rise.
ww.No change in the market: A binding price ceiling changes the market by creating a gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied, so saying there is no change is wrong.
ww.A surplus of rental housing: A surplus needs quantity supplied above quantity demanded, but a low maximum rent raises demand and lowers supply, so the result is a shortage, not a surplus.

rw: A price floor above the market price raises quantity supplied and lowers quantity demanded, so more crop is produced than buyers want, creating a surplus.

ww.A shortage of the crop: A shortage requires demand above supply; a minimum price above equilibrium reduces quantity demanded and increases quantity supplied, so it creates a surplus, not a shortage.
ww.A fall in the price of the crop: A minimum price above the market price keeps the price higher, not lower, so it cannot cause the price of the crop to fall.
ww.No effect: A binding price floor interferes with the market, changing the quantities supplied and demanded, so it has an effect, namely a surplus of the crop.

rw: A rent control law that caps monthly rent is a price ceiling, because it sets a legal maximum price that landlords may charge for housing.

ww.A subsidy for farmers, which is paid by: A farm subsidy is a payment to producers to lower their costs, not a legal limit on price, so it is not a price ceiling.
ww.A tax on tobacco: A tax on tobacco raises costs and prices, but it is not a legal limit on what sellers may charge, so it is not a price ceiling.
ww.A minimum wage law: A minimum wage law sets a lowest legal price for labor, which makes it a price floor, not a ceiling that caps a maximum price.

rw: A minimum wage law sets the lowest legal price for labor, so it is a price floor that prevents wages from falling below a set level.

ww.A rent control law: Rent control caps the price landlords can charge, which is a maximum price and therefore a price ceiling, not a floor.
ww.A cap on gasoline prices: A cap on gasoline prices limits how high the price can go, which is a price ceiling, not a floor that stops prices falling.
ww.A price limit on medicine: A price limit on medicine sets a maximum amount sellers may charge, so it is a price ceiling, not a price floor.

rw: The three types commonly described are frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch) and cyclical (caused by weak economic activity), which together explain most unemployment.

ww.Frictional, financial and fiscal, each o: Financial and fiscal are not types of unemployment; the three commonly described types are frictional, structural and cyclical, each with its own cause.
ww.Seasonal, social and structural: Seasonal unemployment is a recognized type, but social is not a type of unemployment, so this set of three does not match the common classification.
ww.Cyclical, circular and civil: Cyclical is a real type, but circular and civil are not types of unemployment, so this list is wrong.

rw: Frictional unemployment occurs when workers are between jobs or searching for a better fit, as with a graduate who is looking for the right position.

ww.Structural: Structural unemployment comes from skills no longer matching jobs, but a graduate between jobs is simply searching for a better fit, which is frictional.
ww.Seasonal: Seasonal unemployment follows predictable yearly patterns such as holiday or farm work, but this graduate is searching for a better match, not facing a season.
ww.Cyclical: Cyclical unemployment arises from a weak economy and general job losses, but the graduate is only searching for a better fit, which is frictional.

rw: Structural unemployment occurs when workers' skills no longer match available jobs, often after technology or industry changes, as happened to these factory workers.

ww.Cyclical: Cyclical unemployment comes from a downturn in the economy, but these workers lost jobs because their skills no longer match available jobs, which is structural.
ww.Seasonal: Seasonal unemployment follows predictable times of year, but nothing in the scenario links the job losses to a season; it concerns a skills mismatch instead.
ww.Frictional: Frictional unemployment is brief searching between jobs, but these workers lack skills the market needs, which makes their unemployment structural.

rw: Cyclical unemployment occurs when the economy slows and firms cut jobs because demand for goods falls, which matches workers losing jobs during a downturn.

ww.Frictional: Frictional unemployment is temporary job searching, but job losses from a general economic slowdown are cyclical in nature.
ww.Structural: Structural unemployment results from a skills mismatch or industry change, but job losses from a general economic slowdown are cyclical.
ww.Seasonal: Seasonal unemployment follows predictable times of year, but a slowing economy is not a seasonal pattern, so this scenario describes cyclical unemployment.

rw: Seasonal unemployment occurs when work depends on the time of year, and ski instructors have little to do in summer when there is no snow.

ww.Structural: Structural unemployment arises from skills mismatch or industry change, but ski instructors idle in summer are out of work because of the time of year.
ww.Cyclical: Cyclical unemployment follows the business cycle and economic downturns, but ski instructors lose work each summer regardless of how the economy is performing.
ww.Frictional: Frictional unemployment is brief searching between jobs, but ski instructors are out of work because the season ends, not because they are looking for a better match.

rw: The labor force is made up of people who are employed or actively seeking work, so it includes both employed and unemployed people who want to work.

ww.All people in the country: The labor force does not include everyone in the country; children, retirees, students and others not seeking work are excluded from this group.
ww.Only people with full-time jobs: The labor force includes part-time workers and people seeking jobs, not only those with full-time jobs, so limiting it to full-time workers is wrong.
ww.Only people with a college degree who ar: No degree is required to be in the labor force; anyone employed or actively looking for work counts, whatever their education level.

rw: The unemployment rate is unemployed divided by labor force, so 10 million divided by 200 million equals 0.05, or 5 percent.

ww.210 percent, found by adding: Adding 200 and 10 gives 210, but a rate is a share found by dividing, and no unemployment rate can be above 100 percent here.
ww.20 percent, found by dividing the labor: Dividing the labor force by the unemployed gives 200 divided by 10, which equals 20, but the formula is unemployed divided by labor force.
ww.10 percent, found by treating the number: Treating 10 million as 10 percent ignores the labor force of 200 million; the correct division is 10 divided by 200, which is 5 percent.

rw: The Consumer Price Index measures changes in the prices of a basket of goods and services bought by typical households, and is used to calculate inflation.

ww.The total value of goods produced in the: Total value of goods produced in a year is GDP, not CPI; the CPI tracks consumer prices for a typical basket of goods.
ww.The interest rate: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing money and is not what the CPI measures; the CPI tracks changes in the prices of goods.
ww.The number of jobs: The number of jobs is an employment statistic; the Consumer Price Index measures how prices for a basket of goods and services change.

rw: Inflation is the percentage change in the index: 210 minus 200 equals 10, and 10 divided by 200 equals 0.05, which is 5 percent.

ww.2 percent, found by moving the decimal: Moving the decimal does not give an inflation rate; the rate is the change in the index divided by the old index, 10 divided by 200, equal to 5 percent.
ww.10 percent, found by using the change as: Using the change of 10 as a percent ignores the starting level of 200; the inflation rate is 10 divided by 200, which equals 5 percent.
ww.210 percent, found by using the new inde: Using the new index of 210 as a percent confuses a level with a rate of change; the rate is the increase relative to the old index.

rw: Deflation is a general fall in prices over time, which raises the purchasing power of money but can discourage spending and hurt business profits.

ww.A rise in wages: A rise in wages is not deflation, which refers to the general price level; wages can rise while prices stay stable or even fall.
ww.A general rise in prices over a period o: A general rise in prices that makes each dollar buy less is inflation, which is the opposite of deflation, where prices fall.
ww.A fall in output: A fall in output describes a recession or contraction; deflation is about the general price level falling, not about the amount of production.

rw: Stagflation is high inflation together with high unemployment and slow growth, a rare combination, as seen in the 1970s oil shock years.

ww.A fall in the stock market only: A stock market fall is a financial event, not stagflation, which is a combination of high inflation, high unemployment and slow growth in the economy.
ww.Low inflation with low unemployment and: Low inflation, low unemployment and fast growth describes a healthy economy, the opposite of stagflation, which pairs rising prices with weak output and high joblessness.
ww.Rapid growth with falling prices: Rapid growth with falling prices is the opposite of stagflation, which combines slow growth, high unemployment and rising prices, so this does not fit.

rw: A depression is a severe and prolonged downturn in economic activity, with falling output, high unemployment and lost income lasting years, like the 1930s Great Depression.

ww.A fall in the price of one product in a: A price fall for one product in one local market is a minor event; a depression is a severe, prolonged downturn across the whole economy.
ww.A short slowdown of a few weeks: A short slowdown of a few weeks is too brief to count; a depression is a severe downturn lasting years, much deeper than a normal recession.
ww.A time of rapid growth: A time of rapid growth is an economic boom, the opposite of a depression, which involves falling output and widespread unemployment.

rw: GDP stands for gross domestic product, the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.

ww.Government debt payment: Government debt payment is not what the initials stand for; GDP is gross domestic product, a measure of total output in a country.
ww.General domestic prices: General domestic prices does not match the initials; GDP stands for gross domestic product, which measures the value of goods and services produced.
ww.Gross dollar profit: Gross dollar profit is not a real economic term; GDP means gross domestic product, which measures output rather than profit in dollars.

rw: A new car produced and sold this year is a final good made in the current period, so its value is counted in that year's GDP.

ww.Money gifted between friends, which is n: Gifts between friends are transfers with no production or market sale, so they add nothing to the output measured by GDP.
ww.A stock purchase: A stock purchase is a transfer of ownership of a financial asset, not production of a new good or service, so GDP excludes it.
ww.A used car resold this year: A used car resold this year was produced in an earlier year, so counting it again would be double counting; only new production is included.

rw: Intermediate goods are left out to avoid counting the same value twice, since their value is already included in the price of the final good.

ww.They have no value: Intermediate goods do have value; they are left out because their value is already included in the final good, not because they are worthless.
ww.They are illegal: Intermediate goods are legal products used in making other goods, such as steel for cars, so illegality is not the reason they are excluded.
ww.They are produced only in other countrie: Intermediate goods are made at home as well as abroad, so being produced only in other countries cannot be why GDP leaves them out.

rw: The four expenditure components are consumption, investment, government spending and net exports, which together add up to the total spending on the economy's output.

ww.Land, labor, capital and enterprise, whi: Land, labor, capital and enterprise are the factors of production, inputs used to make goods, not the spending components of GDP.
ww.Savings, taxes, debt and credit: Savings, taxes, debt and credit are financial concepts, not the spending categories that make up GDP in the expenditure approach.
ww.Wages, rent, interest and profit: Wages, rent, interest and profit are the income approach categories of GDP, not the four spending components of the expenditure approach.

rw: GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, so 700 plus 200 plus 300 plus negative 50 equals 1,150 billion dollars.

ww.$1,200 billion, found by adding net expo: Adding net exports would give 1,200 only if net exports were positive 50; here they are negative 50, so they must be subtracted, giving 1,150.
ww.$700 billion, which is consumption only: Consumption alone is only one part of GDP; investment of 200 and government spending of 300 must be added, and net exports of negative 50 subtracted.
ww.$1,250 billion, found by ignoring net ex: Ignoring net exports gives 700 plus 200 plus 300, which equals 1,200, not 1,250; net exports of negative 50 must be included, leaving 1,150.

rw: Real GDP is GDP adjusted for inflation, using constant prices, so it shows true changes in output rather than increases caused only by higher prices.

ww.GDP before any adjustment for inflation: GDP not adjusted for inflation is nominal GDP, which is measured at current prices; real GDP removes the effect of price changes.
ww.GDP of a rich country: Real GDP has nothing to do with whether a country is rich; it is a measure of output after adjusting for changes in prices.
ww.GDP in a foreign currency: Converting GDP to a foreign currency is an exchange rate matter, not an inflation adjustment, so it does not define real GDP.

rw: Real GDP growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation, so 6 percent minus 2 percent equals about 4 percent, after removing the effect of higher prices.

ww.About 3 percent, found by dividing: Dividing 6 by 2 gives 3, but real growth is found by subtracting the price increase from nominal growth, which gives 6 minus 2 equals 4.
ww.About 12 percent, found by multiplying: Multiplying 6 by 2 gives 12, but real growth subtracts inflation from nominal growth; the correct figure is 6 minus 2 equals 4 percent.
ww.About 8 percent, found by adding: Adding 6 and 2 gives 8, but inflation is removed from nominal growth, not added; the correct calculation is 6 minus 2, equal to 4 percent.

rw: GDP per capita is GDP divided by the population, which shows average output per person and is used to compare living standards across countries.

ww.GDP multiplied by population, which give: Multiplying GDP by population gives a meaningless huge number; GDP per capita is found by dividing GDP by the population to get output per person.
ww.GDP minus taxes: Subtracting taxes from GDP gives something like disposable income, not a per-person measure; per capita means divided by the number of people.
ww.GDP of one sector: GDP of one sector is a sector's output, not a per-person average; per capita requires dividing the whole economy's GDP by its population.

rw: Cutting taxes and raising government spending to boost demand during a recession is expansionary fiscal policy, because it increases spending and output in the economy.

ww.Expansionary monetary policy: Monetary policy is run by the central bank using interest rates and money supply, while cutting taxes and raising spending are done by government, which is fiscal policy.
ww.Trade policy: Trade policy concerns tariffs, quotas and trade agreements, not taxes and government spending, so it does not describe the response to a recession.
ww.Contractionary fiscal policy: Contractionary fiscal policy raises taxes or cuts spending to slow the economy, the opposite of cutting taxes and raising spending during a recession.

rw: Lowering interest rates to encourage borrowing and spending is expansionary monetary policy, since the central bank acts to stimulate economic activity.

ww.Contractionary monetary policy: Contractionary monetary policy would raise interest rates to discourage borrowing, the opposite of the Fed lowering rates to encourage it.
ww.Expansionary fiscal policy: Fiscal policy involves government taxes and spending decisions, while the Fed changing interest rates is monetary policy, so this is not fiscal.
ww.Trade policy: Trade policy covers tariffs and trade agreements, not interest rates, so lowering rates to encourage borrowing is not a trade policy.

rw: The Fed typically raises interest rates in response to high inflation, which makes borrowing costlier, slows spending and reduces upward pressure on prices.

ww.It prints more money without limit: Printing more money without limit would raise inflation further, not lower it, so it is not how the Fed responds to high inflation.
ww.It bans price increases: Banning price increases is a price control the Fed has no authority to impose, and it would cause shortages, so it is not a typical response.
ww.It lowers interest rates: Lowering interest rates makes borrowing cheaper and boosts spending, which would add to inflation, so the Fed does the opposite when inflation is high.

rw: A budget deficit occurs when government spending exceeds its revenue in a year, so the government must borrow to cover the gap between what it spends and collects.

ww.A balanced budget: A balanced budget means spending equals revenue, so there is no gap and no deficit, which is the opposite of what is being asked.
ww.The total owed by the government, which: The total owed from earlier deficits is the national debt, which accumulates over time, while a deficit is the shortfall in a single year.
ww.When revenue exceeds spending: Revenue exceeding spending is a budget surplus, not a deficit, since the government takes in more than it spends that year.

rw: The national debt is the total amount the government owes, built up from past borrowing to cover deficits, and includes bonds held by investors and others.

ww.The yearly shortfall: The yearly shortfall is the budget deficit, a flow measured over one year, whereas the national debt is the accumulated total owed.
ww.The amount the government spends in one: The amount spent in one year is government spending, not debt; the national debt is what accumulates from borrowing over many years.
ww.The money in the treasury: Money in the treasury is government cash holdings, an asset, whereas the national debt is a liability showing what the government owes lenders.

rw: Each country should specialize where its opportunity cost is lower, so A makes cloth and B makes wheat, then they trade, giving both more of both goods.

ww.Neither should trade: If neither country trades, both lose the gains from specialization; comparative advantage shows each can be better off by specializing and trading.
ww.Each should make both goods: Making both goods ignores comparative advantage; each country gains by concentrating on the good with the lower opportunity cost and trading for the other.
ww.A should make wheat and B should make cl: This reverses the correct assignment, because A has the lower opportunity cost in cloth, not wheat, so A should make cloth and B should make wheat.

rw: Absolute advantage is the ability to produce more of a good with the same resources than another producer can, so output per unit of input is higher.

ww.The ability to produce at a lower opport: Producing at a lower opportunity cost is comparative advantage, not absolute advantage, which compares how much each country can produce with the same resources.
ww.The ability to avoid taxes: Avoiding taxes is a legal or accounting matter and says nothing about production; absolute advantage compares the output possible with the same resources.
ww.The ability to charge higher prices: Charging higher prices is a market behavior, not a production ability; absolute advantage concerns producing more with the same resources.

rw: A stronger dollar buys more euros, so Europeans must pay more euros for the same American goods, making exports more expensive for them.

ww.They stop: American exports do not stop when the dollar strengthens; they continue but become pricier for Europeans, so quantity sold may fall, not drop to nothing.
ww.They become cheaper for Europeans, since: The reasoning is backwards, because a stronger dollar means Europeans need more euros to buy dollars, so American goods become more expensive for Europeans, not cheaper.
ww.They are unaffected: Exchange rates change the foreign price of American goods, so exports are affected; a stronger dollar makes them costlier for Europeans.

rw: Multiplying 200 dollars by 0.90 euros per dollar gives 180 euros, which is the amount you receive when converting at that rate.

ww.222 euros, found by dividing by 0.90: Dividing 200 by 0.90 gives about 222, but each dollar buys 0.90 euros, so you multiply 200 by 0.90 to get 180.
ww.200 euros, ignoring the rate: Ignoring the rate would give 200 euros, but one dollar buys only 0.90 euros, so 200 dollars buys 180 euros, not 200.
ww.20 euros, found by moving the decimal: Moving the decimal gives 20, which is not based on the exchange rate; multiply 200 by 0.90 to get 180 euros.

rw: A free trade agreement is an agreement among countries to reduce tariffs and other trade barriers, so goods and services move more freely between them.

ww.A ban on trade: A ban on trade is the opposite of free trade; a free trade agreement removes or reduces barriers so goods can cross borders more easily.
ww.A rule that sets prices: A rule that sets prices is a price control, which is unrelated to trade agreements that lower barriers between countries.
ww.A tax on imports: A tax on imports is a tariff, which is a trade barrier; a free trade agreement reduces such tariffs instead of imposing them.

rw: Protectionism is a set of policies, such as tariffs and quotas, that restrict imports to shield domestic industries from foreign competition.

ww.Policies that protect the environment: Protecting the environment is environmental policy, which is unrelated to trade policy; protectionism concerns restricting imports to help domestic industries.
ww.Policies that remove all barriers: Removing all barriers to trade is free trade, the opposite of protectionism, which adds barriers such as tariffs and quotas.
ww.Policies that protect consumers from fra: Rules against false advertising are consumer protection laws, which are not trade policy; protectionism specifically restricts imports to protect domestic producers.

rw: A monopsony is a market with a single buyer, such as one employer in a small town buying labor, which gives it power to set low wages.

ww.A market with two sellers: A market with two sellers is a duopoly, a form of oligopoly; monopsony is about buyers, not sellers, so this option does not fit.
ww.A market with many buyers and sellers: Many buyers and sellers describes a competitive market; monopsony has only one buyer, which gives that buyer power over prices.
ww.A market with a single seller: A single seller is a monopoly; a monopsony is the reverse, with one buyer facing many sellers.

rw: Perfect competition has many sellers of identical products and easy entry, so no single firm can influence price and all sellers accept the market price.

ww.A market with price controls only: Price controls only are government interventions, not a market structure; perfect competition is defined by many sellers, identical products and easy entry.
ww.A market with one seller: A market with one seller is a monopoly, which is the opposite extreme from perfect competition, where many sellers compete.
ww.A market with a few large sellers, each: A few large sellers watching rivals' prices describes an oligopoly; perfect competition has many small sellers who cannot influence the price.

rw: Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering differentiated products, such as restaurants or clothing brands, which gives each firm a limited ability to set its own price.

ww.A market with identical products, where: Identical products where no seller can differ in price describes perfect competition; monopolistic competition features differentiated products, which let firms charge somewhat different prices.
ww.A market with one seller: A market with one seller is a monopoly, not monopolistic competition, which has many sellers.
ww.A market with two sellers: A market with two sellers is a duopoly, not monopolistic competition, which has many sellers with differentiated products.

rw: A negative externality is a cost imposed on others who are not part of a transaction, such as pollution from a factory harming nearby residents.

ww.A benefit received by others: A benefit received by others is a positive externality, the opposite of a negative externality, which imposes costs on people outside the transaction.
ww.A tax paid by firms: A tax paid by firms is a government charge, not a spillover effect; negative externalities are costs that fall on third parties.
ww.A loss in profit: A loss in profit is a cost to the firm itself, whereas a negative externality is a cost imposed on outsiders.

rw: A positive externality is a benefit received by people not part of a transaction, such as a vaccine's protection of others who did not pay for it.

ww.A subsidy: A subsidy is a government payment, sometimes used to encourage positive externalities, but it is not the externality itself, which is a benefit to third parties.
ww.A profit: A profit is a gain to the firm, not a spillover to outsiders, while a positive externality is a benefit received by people outside the transaction.
ww.A cost imposed on others: A cost imposed on others is a negative externality, the opposite of a positive externality, which gives benefits to outsiders.

rw: A pollution tax makes producers pay for the harm they cause and reduces output, so the cost of the externality is built into the price.

ww.To increase pollution, so that firms mus: Taxing pollution aims to reduce it, not increase it; raising tax revenue is a side effect and does not describe the reason.
ww.To help the polluter: A pollution tax charges polluters for the harm they cause, so it hurts rather than helps them and is intended to reduce pollution.
ww.To lower prices: A pollution tax raises the cost of production, which tends to raise prices rather than lower them, so lowering prices is not its aim.

rw: The free rider problem occurs when people benefit from a good without paying for it, which makes it hard for markets to supply public goods.

ww.People pay more than their fair share of: Paying more than a fair share is the opposite of free riding, which involves paying nothing or less than your share while still benefiting.
ww.People ride for free on a bus: Free riding is an economic concept about avoiding payment for benefits, not about riding a bus; the term is not literal.
ww.People refuse to buy a good: Refusing to buy a good is a decision not to consume, whereas free riders do consume the benefits while avoiding payment.

rw: A sunk cost is a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, so it should not influence future decisions.

ww.A cost of ships: A cost of ships is a play on the word sunk and is not an economic definition; sunk costs are costs already paid.
ww.A cost expected next year: A cost expected next year is a future cost, which can still be changed; a sunk cost is one already incurred.
ww.A cost that can be avoided by changing p: A cost that can be avoided is a future or avoidable cost; a sunk cost has already been paid, so it cannot be avoided.

rw: The 50,000 dollars is a sunk cost that cannot be recovered, so the company should base its decision on future costs and revenues, which show the product loses money.

ww.Keep spending because $50,000 was alread: Continuing to spend because of money already invested commits the sunk cost fallacy, since the 50,000 dollars is gone whatever happens next.
ww.Double the spending: Doubling the spending adds more losses to a product that will lose money, and ignores that the earlier 50,000 dollars is already gone.
ww.Ignore the future: Ignoring the future is wrong, since decisions should depend on future costs and revenues; only the past, sunk spending should be ignored.

rw: Marginal analysis compares the extra benefit of an action with its extra cost, and a person should act when marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.

ww.Comparing past and present: Comparing past and present is a trend comparison, not marginal analysis, which looks at the additional benefit and cost of one more unit.
ww.Comparing total costs only, without look: Comparing total costs only leaves out the extra benefit, so it is not marginal analysis, which weighs additional benefit against additional cost.
ww.Comparing two firms: Comparing two firms is a competitor comparison and is unrelated to marginal analysis, which compares extra benefits and extra costs of an action.

rw: Diminishing marginal utility means each additional unit gives less satisfaction than the one before, which matches the seventh slice of pizza being less enjoyable than the sixth.

ww.Constant utility: Constant utility would mean each slice gives the same satisfaction, but the seventh slice gives less than the sixth, so utility is not constant.
ww.Increasing marginal utility, since each: Increasing marginal utility would mean each extra slice gives more satisfaction than the last, but the seventh gives less, so the pattern is the reverse.
ww.Perfect competition: Perfect competition is a market structure and has nothing to do with the satisfaction a person gets from eating slices of pizza.

rw: Utility in economics is the satisfaction or benefit a person gets from consuming a good or service, which helps explain why consumers choose what they buy.

ww.The cost of electricity: The cost of electricity is a price paid for power, not an economic definition of utility, which refers to satisfaction from consuming goods.
ww.A public service company: A public service company is a utility company in everyday speech, but in economics utility means satisfaction, not a type of firm.
ww.The profit of a firm: The profit of a firm is revenue minus costs, while utility measures the satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming a good.

rw: Each cake gives a contribution of 20 minus 8, which is 12 dollars, so break-even is 1,200 divided by 12, which equals 100 cakes.

ww.150 cakes, found by dividing fixed costs: Dividing fixed costs by variable cost gives 1,200 divided by 8, which equals 150, but break-even requires dividing by the 12 dollar contribution per cake.
ww.1,200 cakes, found by using fixed costs: Using fixed costs of 1,200 as a number of units confuses dollars with cakes; break-even is 1,200 divided by the 12 dollar contribution, which is 100 cakes.
ww.60 cakes, found by dividing fixed costs: Dividing fixed costs by price gives 1,200 divided by 20, which equals 60, but each cake covers variable cost, so contribution of 12 is used, giving 100.

rw: Revenue is 400 times 4, which equals 1,600 dollars; subtracting costs of 1,300 gives a monthly profit of 300 dollars.

ww.$2,900, found by adding: Adding revenue and costs gives 1,600 plus 1,300, which is 2,900, but profit is revenue minus costs, so the correct figure is 300 dollars.
ww.$1,300, which is cost: Costs of 1,300 are not profit; profit is revenue minus costs, and revenue of 1,600 minus 1,300 leaves 300 dollars.
ww.$1,600, which is revenue: Revenue of 400 cups times 4 dollars is 1,600, but profit subtracts the 1,300 costs, leaving 300 dollars rather than 1,600.

rw: Contribution margin per unit is selling price minus variable cost, so 25 minus 10 equals 15 dollars, which is available to cover fixed costs and profit.

ww.$10, which is the variable cost: The variable cost of 10 dollars is what each unit costs to make, whereas contribution margin is price minus variable cost, which is 25 minus 10, equal to 15.
ww.$35, found by adding: Adding price and variable cost gives 35, but contribution margin subtracts variable cost from the selling price, so it is 25 minus 10 equals 15 dollars.
ww.$2.50, found by dividing: Dividing 25 by 10 gives 2.50, which is a ratio and not a dollar margin; contribution margin is found by subtracting, giving 15 dollars.
